utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances -- sorry. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and good morning to my learned friends from the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, we represent Mr. Naser Oric. And together with us, our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to your team. Can we bring in the witness, or are there preliminary matters you wish to address? The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just a short one to hand over, Your Honours, the documents I promised at the end of the private session on Monday, to hand over to the Court and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that include --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Defence counsel has already the copies, and I will not go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that include the aerial map with the two buildings you were interested in being shown or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is at the end of the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are to guess where those two buildings are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you assign a P number to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that's what we are going to do. I take it that you confirm that you have these documents, Mr. Jones? Yes. Do you agree these are two documents, Mr. Wubben, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start -- Madam Registrar, can you follow? Let's start with the first one, and this is a one-page document in each of the two languages, B/C/S and English, bearing ERN number 03642076. This is given exhibit number P ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 494, P494. And the second document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P495.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, which will be given exhibit number P495. Consists of a document which starts with ERN 03639227 until 03639244, in both languages. Yes, are you ready, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a preliminary. Perhaps we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be proceeding with your examination-in-chief. Yes. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will start my questions regarding an issue of uniforms, wearing uniforms. We already addressed that issue yesterday. Yesterday, you clarified to the Judges wearing uniforms, also to be used for the military actions in the various areas. Your testimony also referred to special forces operating during those military actions. Now, my question is: Did these special forces that you mentioned also wear uniforms, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was talking about special units, I didn't mean special units in the sense of a well-organised unit. Such a unit was always made of individuals, of those fighters who were ready at that moment to carry out a task. Their uniforms were the same as the uniforms of other troops. It was not an established unit. It was not dressed or armed differently than other members of the armed forces of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did these units, these special units, also wear bands or ribbons?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore bands as well as the others. This was a recognition sign, the sign by which they recognised each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Where do these bands or ribbons, if you may use that word, come from?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took those bands from a factory which was in Zenica. The name of that factory was Vezionica. Its main activity was to manufacture clothes, bridal dresses, night wear, bed linen, and similar things. This factory stopped working at the beginning of the war, and it still had some cloth on the stock, and this material was used during the war. We used it for dressing wounds and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This village where this factory is located is near Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in Srebrenica, some 300 metres before the hospital as you approach Srebrenica from the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can I take it, if so, that prior to an attack or a military action, those bands were circulated, were given to the units involved?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And who distributed those bands or ribbons?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Yesterday, I said whenever I got a wounded soldiers, they always wore those bands. And the colours of those bands differed from one action to another. One time they were white; the other, they were light blue or pink, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And where did you get the bands from? Who distributed the bands to you, your hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received cloth from that factory, and then we used that cloth to make dressing and material that we used to dress the wounds. It was not Dr. Hasanovic who did that; he was the hospital director. But he was in charge of the logistics of the hospital, so he was in charge of all the supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Another issue, Dr. Mujkanovic. During your stay in Srebrenica, August 1992, April 1993, did you notice any storage houses or facilities where various goods had been stored?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a depot or a warehouse which I saw for the first time in the second half of September, in Srebrenica. This was a depot in the part of town called Petrica. I believe that this is where the warehouse was, at the very beginning of that part of the town. This was a building which, probably even before the war, used to be used as a warehouse or a storage, because that's how it was designed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was that the only storage house or storage facility?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, towards the end of November and the beginning of December, or even the end of November, the first humanitarian convoy entered Zenica. It was followed by another one seven days later. This convoy brought food, blankets, and some other things that were needed by the people. They also brought some supplies for the war hospital, some gauzes, some medicines, and so on and so forth. In the department store called Srebrenica, in the centre of town, another storage facility was opened in order to accommodate all those supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And in Potocari, was there also a storage facility or a storage house?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no official storage facility to store food or other supplies in Potocari. There were only the two that I have just mentioned in the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And was there a more unofficial storage house in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about unofficial storage facilities. However, in my conversations with the troops, I learned that, in Naser Oric's house, or the house where he lived, there was a storage and that is where some of the ammunition was kept. So this was in his own house. There was also some food storage there, and this all served for the purposes of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What purposes of the army? Can you please clarify to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a reserve stock for the fighters. This is where they got their food from. Yesterday, I said that the biggest problem in Srebrenica was the lack of food, and that the lack of food made people to go into actions, to obtain food. Those fighters who participated in the fighting did not have the time to obtain food, so this storage was used to supply food to extremely courageous people who fought in those actions. So the most extremely courageous people would obtain food for themselves and for their families from this place, from this unofficial storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And who allowed those extremely courageous soldiers to receive food from that storage in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, and according to what I heard, this storage was in Naser Oric's house. Who was in charge of the storage itself, I don't know. I was never there, and I didn't know how this food was distributed, and in what quantities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did Naser Oric give permission to distribute food according to the purposes you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. I would not venture to provide any answer to something like that. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When it comes to the other storage facilities, what kind of supplies had been stored over there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other storages were under the control of the War Presidency and the civilian protection of Srebrenica. They contained some food and some other things, such as blankets, clothes. They were usually half empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And who secured the storage depot at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Potocari. I was never there. I'm just telling you what I heard. I was not there. I can tell you something about the storage facility in Petrica, where I went on two or three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And my next question is: Where did these goods come from? I mean the food, blankets, clothes.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the convoy arrived in Srebrenica towards the end of November, and the next one which came at the beginning of December, those were the only two convoys. The next one after that arrived at the beginning of April 1993. These convoys brought clothes, blankets, and similar things, and they also brought flour, oil, some sugar, some tinned food, cheese, and so on and so forth. Before that, the villages which were around Srebrenica were obliged to provide a certain quantity of food for the hospital, and that food was stored in the storage facility in Petrica. In other words, from all the villages, people would bring food. Somebody would bring corn flour, somebody else would bring marmalade, somebody else would bring lard. This was just something that the population did in order to provide for the normal functioning of the hospital. People also brought milk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And is it knowledge -- and is it your knowledge whether or not these goods also were brought in after some military actions, like goods looted by participants in the actions?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such food was brought into these storage facilities after military operations, because the houses had already been looted by civilians going to and fro. But I don't know how they organised, what sort of an arrangement they had in the villages, because they had had to set aside apart of the staple foods for the purposes of the army -- of the military. Probably some foods obtained by civilians in such a way ended up in the hospital. However, the civilians, the villagers, had the obligation to set aside some of the foods that were then transported to the hospital, and that was used for patients. I can tell you that Srebrenica used to have some 200, 300, 400 wounded at a time, so that some of the wounded in the beginning were put up in the Hotel Domavija, and others in the sanitary facility. And that was the only source of food for these wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So, Dr. Mujkanovic, is it your testimony that storage facilities in Srebrenica at that time had to serve both civilians and military, and the storage house of Naser Oric had the purpose for the army?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time these storage facilities were used for the purposes of the hospital and some exceptionally vulnerable population in Srebrenica, the elderly, who were unable to come by food in any other way and were thus issued with a certain amount of food to enable them to survive, whereas the villages themselves, they were there to provide food for the military. I was trying to explain to you that the units were not billeted in any barracks. The troops stayed in their own respective homes and would then go to take up their positions at the front line and would then be replaced by others and return home. And this is how it functioned, on a rotational basis, but more as village guards rather than well-established units. The troops, therefore, had their meals at their own homes, and nobody had to assume responsibility for feeding them and arming them. Whatever they were able to come by themselves, they would have at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And this practice was your experience -- consistent with your experience from August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will move to another issue. But before, I have a short question again about these uniforms. Whenever they were uniforms wearing, was that also -- and I know that you confirmed to the Judges that only a small percentage were wearing uniforms. But was there also a possibility of white winter uniforms that the soldiers wore?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Have you ever seen those?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When did you see them?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the soldiers that I used to see wearing these white winter uniforms, which were basically camouflage uniforms, but there was a sort of overcoat that was placed on the clothes that they had on themselves, and these uniforms were actually tailored and sewn in the manufacturing plant that I mentioned earlier on, Vezionica. Those were the ones that I saw, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And when you saw those uniforms, can I take it that that was, indeed, wintertime?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. It was wintertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Snowing?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Snowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can I take it that that was the end of December or beginning of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Wubben, Your Honours, in Srebrenica, the snow falls in October and melts in April, so basically half of the year we are covered in snow. That's the sort of climate we have there. And that's what made the lives of the population there even more difficult, the fact that there was this harsh wintertime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Dr. Mujkanovic. That's why I focussed on the month. Do you recall what month or time you saw those white uniforms wearing?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in December, January, February, March.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you testified about a document regarding the resignation of the staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica. Did that list, as you recall, and this is just refreshing -- that list of resigning staff, also include Hamid Salihovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Hamid Salihovic listed first yesterday, and then Ramiz Becirevic, and then I don't recall who the other ones were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I would like to have now the assistance of the usher for document P200. Your Honours, it's -- the translation in English is on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This is a document, ERN number 03721253. It's dated, Srebrenica, 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And my first question is to you, Dr. Mujkanovic: Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature does look like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you please follow the procedure that we adopted yesterday, and on previous occasions, to put it for a short while on the ELMO so that the public can see which signature we're talking about. Yes. I thank you. Witness, you have seen this signature also on the ELMO. Could I ask you to repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This signature does look like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, we have an interpretation issue. The witness always uses the term, I think it's slicni, which we understand resembles, when the interpreters say "does look like," to us that implies an emphasis which this witness isn't -- isn't stating. He's saying it resembles -- it's simply that -- perhaps the interpreters could be heavy on that. As we understand it, it's weaker, slicni is, it resembles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're understanding it as resembling. At least from my point of view, I'm not laying any emphasis on the "does." "Looks like" is "resemble," in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A positive affirmation, in other words, what he's saying, that there is a resemblance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there's a resemblance, it resembles, it looks like, something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, point taken, but don't worry about it, Mr. Jones. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My next question relates to the content of this document. Please, Dr. Mujkanovic, will you read it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This is, and I will resume, an order that Hamid Salihovic is being relieved of the duty of the chief for intelligence and security affairs. My question is: What is your comment in respect to the resignation by Hamid Salihovic as shown in the letter of resignation done in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I've already told you yesterday: Resignation is an act. By saying that you will resign, it doesn't necessarily mean that you will, in actual fact, resign. Hamid Salihovic and other members of the operations staff who signed some sort of a resignation continued performing their duties until they were actually relieved of their duties and assigned to different duties. And this document proves it, that Hamid Salihovic was -- until the 16th of April, 1993, meaning for some four, five months after he had actually handed in his resignation, continued performing his functions within the operations staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move to another issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, do you know whether or not there was, at your time, at your stay in Srebrenica, any exchanges of Serb prisoners or detainees?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not attend any exchanges, nor was I aware of the persons being exchanged. But I did know that there were some meetings led by, chaired by Atif Ustic. These were meetings taking place between Srebrenica and Bratunac, speaking in geographical terms, related to the exchange of dead bodies on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can I take it that this Atif Ustic was in charge of the exchange? Is that your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, he negotiated and ran these exchanges, because I recall this one dead body that was exchanged for a soldier who belongs to his unit. And that's how I know that exchanges took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You stayed for eight and a half months in Srebrenica. Was Atif Ustic all the time in charge of the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He didn't say he was in charge of the exchange. He was asked that question and he didn't accept the suggestion that Atif Ustic was in charge. So that has to be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the objection is well-founded, Mr. Wubben. Perhaps you can phrase your question. It's no big deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Point well taken. I'll withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My question is: Your testimony is that Atif Ustic negotiated with a view to exchange of Serb prisoners or detainees. Did he do that all the time? Was he the person who negotiated all the time during your stay, or was there any change of persons negotiating?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Atif Ustic died in early October 1992. He got killed. So I don't know whether afterwards there was someone who negotiated, officially or unofficially, for the exchange of prisoners and dead bodies. The only thing I do know is that he ran these negotiations until his death, and that I myself witnessed the exchange of one dead body, involving a member of his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you learn from others, perhaps, who the name of his successor was, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was any successor. We have to clarify certain things. Whether Atif Ustic led these exchanges of his own initiative, that is something I don't know either. I only know that he was the one holding talks about it. Later on, there was talk about some people discussing matters, meeting with the Serbs at some sections of the defence line. There was even talk of exchange of goods in certain areas, localities like Zepa, and that they were discussing exchanges of those killed. I also heard that one of the people who used to meet with the Serbs primarily on the issue of exchanging certain goods, and then also, in so doing, discussing the exchanges, I believe he was Ibrahim Mandzic, also known as Mrki. I'm not sure about his first name. I know that he was Mrki Mandzic. But whether this was his own initiative or whether he was an official representative, I cannot say. I only know what I told you, that according to the stories that went around Srebrenica, that he used to meet with the Serbs in some localities along those lines that I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did Naser Oric play any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did Naser Oric play any role in these exchanges of prisoners, Serb prisoners, or detainees, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent I know, he did not play any role, or at least I don't know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Usher, may I have your assistance, please. Exhibit number P99. P99 is, Your Honour, an exhibit with ERN number 00926395.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And the English version is on the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please take a look at this.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've taken a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, do you recognise the signature? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature looks like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It is a letter or note, handwritten, dated the 10th of June, 1992. And I refer -- I will refer with my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Can we put it back on the ELMO, please, and zoom out, not zoom in. Zoom out. Yes. Yes. You have been asked about the signature. Look at the lest of the document, the handwriting that it contains. Does that handwriting look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My question refers to the sentence: "We agree to exchange everyone for everyone." This quoted, "everyone for everyone," are you familiar with this kind of policy or known label? Do you have any comment to that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This expression was frequently used during the aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to the exchanges. This means that all those present on one side are exchanged for all those present on the other side, regardless of what the numbers of these people captured or killed on other side is. So it's not one for one but all for all. There could be 10 people on one side, 15 people on the other, and the exchange would cover them all, regardless of their numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And this was a common practice when it comes to exchanges like this.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the Bosniak side customarily asked for, because usually there were more Bosniaks killed than the Serbs, although I do not claim that this was always the case. There may have been some conditions placed upon the exchanges of the dead bodies. Otherwise, it was -- the practice was all for all, because if it had been any different than this, then it did become a very inhumane practice, if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move now to another document. It's document number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, this last document that we have seen, is the original in the possession of the Prosecution, or do you only have photocopies of the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We have a photocopy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't have the original. In other words, there is no way one can establish whether it's possible or probable that the same ink was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will make an oral submission on that later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I hope to do that today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And one further question: You have not, by any chance, had any examination of that document carried out by an expert to establish whether it's written by the same person in its entirety, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have no knowledge so far in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. So I will include that in that oral submission. 7

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Next one, Your Honour, is P120. Please bear me a moment. It is a document with an ERN number 01787832. The English translation is on Sanction. It's a document dated the 26th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And my question to you, Dr. Mujkanovic: Do you recognise this signature? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature looks like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And in this document, it is referring to a name Veselj Avdic from Voljevica? Do you know that person? Are you familiar with that person, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voljevica. Yes, I am familiar with this person. Veselj Avdic from Voljevica is Naser Oric's father-in-law, that is, Naser's wife's father. I met the man upon my return from Srebrenica, in 1993 or 1994, and I believe he died a few years back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I will move to another document, and that's document P158.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The usher has the English translation. This is a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document dated the 24th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My question is -- oh, ERN number 01239545. My question to you, Dr. Mujkanovic, is: Do you recognise this signature? Whose signature is this?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature looks like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: There is referring in this order to paragraph -- in paragraph 2, or under 2, an appointment of Ejub Golic, commander of the Glogova Independent Battalion. My question is: Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was the position referred to in this appointment consistent with your experience in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ejub Golic was commander of the Glogova before and after. Glogova is a village. I've been telling you about it. It's a village, a pretty large one, and had units at the strength of a battalion. He was commander of Glogova, and I know him as such. But I am not familiar with this appointment or this order. But I do know Ejub Golic as commander of the unit in charge of the village of Glogova, meaning the members of which were villagers of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the date of this document? 24th December, 1992. Dr. Mujkanovic, were there any Muslims still living in Glogova in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Glogova was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wasn't it attacked by the Serbs in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know whether there was an attack in May 1992. I know that Glogova belonged to the municipality of Bratunac, and that in Glogova, either the entire village or parts of the village were occupied by the Serbs. I don't know about that, but I know that there were men from Glogova who were defending either parts of the village or the entire village or half of the village. In any case, people from Glogova were protecting their village, either parts of it or the entire village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're not aware that on the 9th of May, or thereabouts, of 1992, the Serb artillery attacked Glogova, that a number of -- considerable number of Muslims were killed, and practically the whole Muslim population of Glogova was forcibly removed from Glogova, and houses destroyed? You're not aware of that? All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In addition to that, Your Honour, I have a question to Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Are you aware, is it your knowledge, that in December, and that should be the 24th of December, Muslims might have retaken Glogova? The 24th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Glogova was retaken by Muslims. I only know that this man was the commander of Glogova, Ejub Golic. I don't know whether this applied to the entire territory of Glogova, part of it, territories adjacent to Glogova. I really wouldn't be able to tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to clear this up. Is it possible that this battalion you're referring to, the independent -- that the document refers to the independent - can I see the document again, please - the Glogova Independent Battalion was tasked with looking after the interests of Glogova but not based in Glogova? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me something that I cannot clarify, because I don't know it in the way you're asking me. I met Ejub Golic. I knew that he was the commander of Glogova. I don't know whether Glogova was a village retaken, whether it was a village destroyed by the aggressor. But if there was a unit that covered that area, maybe it was adjacent to Glogova, maybe it was not the entire village that was under the control of these fighters from Glogova. I'm sure that they were located in that place, in that locality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doesn't the first paragraph, the one numbered with the number 1, indicate to you that, before the date of this document, the Glogova Independent Battalion did not even exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may not have existed as a battalion, but it existed as a group of village guards or a formation of village guards that existed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben. Thank you. And my apologies to you for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will move to the other document, document P10, P10 with the ERN number, Your Honour, 01239521. I will repeat: 01239521. The English translation is on Sanction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, please take a look at this document dated the 20th of October, 1992, under the heading of "Srebrenica Armed Forces Staff," a list of names under the label of "group pass." Can you take a look at the signature? Whose signature is this? Do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature resembles Naser's signature -- Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I must state that for the good order that this original is double-sided, Your Honour, but I only will refer to the ERN number that I already stated, so it ended up with 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have a question for you, Dr. Mujkanovic, regarding the content of this document, a group pass, and a list of names. Are you familiar with the contents of the issuing of such a group pass, or, at the bottom, the travel from Srebrenica to Tuzla, as referred to?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact that a group of people, and the names that I see here, most of them were sent to Tuzla to try and talk to the district staff of the Territorial Defence in Tuzla and secure logistics for the Srebrenica enclave. And the logistics implied weapons, ammunition, medicines, medical supplies. And this group was supposed to bring some doctors and nurses back to Srebrenica. I know that this group of people, on their return from Tuzla towards Srebrenica, at the beginning of December 1992, the entire group consisted of 100 people. As they were returning from Tuzla to Srebrenica, this group was ambushed near Han Pijesak, and out of the entire group numbering 100 people, only 30 survived. The rest were killed, amongst them, two doctors and all the other paramedics. The remainder of the group, in mid-January, crossed Zepa in the snow. They were taken back. They were frozen when they reached Srebrenica. So, in other words, I am familiar with the entire event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did that request for support or help also include a request for conscripts?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Srebrenica, or the enclave which was called Srebrenica, did not have enough men to put up resistance against the enemy that encircled Srebrenica, and there was always a need to bring fresh men from Tuzla and elsewhere. That's why one of the tasks of that group was to bring people who were ready to come to Srebrenica. Those were usually people who had resided in Srebrenica before the aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when all this was happening, they were residing either in Tuzla or somewhere in the Tuzla region. Amongst other things, a task was to bring new people that would defend Srebrenica. I know that most of these people, I believe that Nurija Memisevic managed to return. Sometime in January, he was brought frozen from Zepa. Salem Mandzic was killed, and actually the majority of people whose names are on this list were killed on that occasion, among them were two doctors. Actually, the entire medical staff was killed in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The following document is P9, a document with the ERN number 01239519. And the English version is on Sanction. Your Honours, this is the last document I will show this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're free to show him more if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This document is dated, Srebrenica, 15th of October, 1992, and I quote in the heading that it is referring to "an improvement of the organisational and establishing of the structure of armed forces units in the free territory of Srebrenica." Then there is the naming of order and formation of brigades and battalions, and at the end, under paragraph 3, units, including, under 3F, a medical company. At the bottom, and I quote: "All unit commanders are hereby assigned to execute this order in cooperation with the armed forces staff immediately, but no later than the 22nd of October, 1992." My first question is: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This signature resembles Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When you take a look, Dr. Mujkanovic, at those brigades, battalions, and units mentioned in this document, this order, is it consistent with your experience that, in the period of your time at Srebrenica, that's August 1992 until April 1993, these brigades, battalions, and units have been formed or established?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this order. I was not aware of this order. The first time I saw it was when the investigators showed it to me. I can only say that the military formations were to be found in the geographic areas that corresponded with certain villages. When you look at this, you will see that this is 100 per cent so. For example, Biljeg here, there was a military organisation there composed of the villagers of Biljeg who manned the defence line there and prevented the break-through of Serbs into that area. If there had been such an order, indeed, it only confirmed the factual situation that existed on the ground. This did not serve to form units. It is not like 200 soldiers were taken from Suceska, 50 from there and 10 from here, to form units. This just confirmed the situation that already existed on the ground. If a village had a company, then it was called a company; if it was a battalion, then it would be called a battalion, for the simple reason that I've already explained to you: There were no logistics to organise the troops in the way they should have been organised. The people were linked to their homes and their lines. The lines that they defended were sometimes 50 metres away from their homes. They would go to the line, to the trench there. After their shift, they would go back home. In other words, this was not an organised army. This army was not structured in any way. I would only be too happy if this functioned in the way it is described here. One would think that this was an organised army, an organised territory, an organised civilian authority. Unfortunately, it wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My question was not referring to the order itself but, indeed, would like to have your comment whether or not these brigades existed at the times of your stay in Srebrenica. Please allow me, Dr. Mujkanovic, to be more specific than in my question. Did, in October 1992, the Potocari Brigade exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to object, but the witness has just given a very lengthy answer on this precise issue. Apart from the slightly leading nature of the question, it invites the response, Well, the Potocari Brigade was -- well, I won't give the evidence. But he's answered this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I -- we need to allow the question put by Mr. Wubben for the following reason: It's true that the witness, in answering the question, the previous question, tried to give as much detail as you like, but he was speaking very generically. And what Mr. Wubben is now trying to extract from the witness is a confirmation, or otherwise, whether the various battalions that are mentioned here were already in existence separately, one by one; in other words, were already in existence more or less in the location shown, although maybe not formally as an enrolled battalion in terms of the decree, law, of the presidency of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, armed forces, et cetera. So basically in as far as he's trying to extract that information from the witness, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. It's just really there's an ambiguity which will creep in, which is that this witness has said that, for him, a battalion means X number of people, a brigade means another number of people. So he may accept, yes, there was a brigade there, by which he means 400 men or something of that nature, and not an organised structure, which is what he's been saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that ambiguity is avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, the question is perfectly legitimate. So, Mr. Wubben, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, can you confirm, according to your knowledge, whether or not the mentioned Potocari Brigade existed in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October 1992, there were units in Potocari. I didn't know that they were called either brigades or battalions. They were not called that way in normal conversations amongst people. Nobody ever mentioned the name, "the brigade of Potocari." The term used was "fighters from Potocari, fighters from Pale, fighters from Bostahovina." We never used formation terms, such as company, battalion, brigade. No such thing existed, and I believe that everybody will confirm this. This is not how the things were. These are not the names we used. If anybody put it on paper, I don't know why they did it. I would only be so happy if this was the real situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My next question is: So there were -- there was a formation in Potocari of fighters, and was this formation also, in part, based in the places mentioned under 1, Gornji Potocari, Gostilj and Pale.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so. That was the line, Potocari, Gostilj, Pale. The line went from one village to another, and the corresponding units bore the corresponding names. There was no need to put battalion 1, battalion 2, battalion 3, because the army was not organised and the formations were not called according to the villages. This implied the area of responsibilities on the defence of Srebrenica. Gornji Potocari and the formation which numbered maybe the number of men that suffice for a battalion covered Gornji Potocari. The next one covered Pale. And these were the men that were members of the units. They stayed at home and then they would go to the lines from their homes, and return home after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it your testimony that the same applies to the formation mentioned in paragraph 1, under B, Suceska Brigade, a formation there, including the places Spasin Do?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Opetci?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opetci these are all villages in the area of Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And the same applies in paragraph number 1, under C?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, these are all the villages, Kragljivoda, Krajcici, and Poljak. This is the south-eastern part of the Srebrenica enclave. These are the villages, and the villagers from these villages made up those units that defended their respective villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And also the same as the formations called as independent battalions mentioned under paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that there were two units in Srebrenica. One was in the town of Srebrenica, Akif Ustic's unit, the name of which is Stari Grad, if memory serves me well, and the other belonged to Kemal [as interpreted] Meholjic which was in the Domavija Hotel. The former one was in Stari Grad, in the very town centre, in the old part of the town. Those were the battalions, and I believe that this refers to them. I cannot be sure of that. But I believe that this refers to these two battalions, because there were no other units in Srebrenica at the time but these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness actually said Hakija Meholjic. It's came out as Kemal Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You just heard what Mr. Jones said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hakija Meholjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The next question is: Does the same apply to the units as mentioned under paragraph 3? And then I mean the units mentioned under A up to E.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See here, from A to E, these are companies, platoons. I am not familiar with the organisation of these companies and platoons, and under F it says medical company. It was never established as a company. I've already told you how this was organised. The war hospital was the centre, and the surgical outposts were in the periphery. And that's how they functioned. I don't know of any medical company as such. Maybe somebody thought that this should be the name used. I've explained how the medical corps functioned. There was no company, there was no company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it's half past. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're starting something new, we'd better stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We should start after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Basically, that means we'll start at five minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will continue with my questions, Dr. Mujkanovic. My next question relates to the leaving of Srebrenica by you, and I take it that was in April 1993; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 22nd of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Who ordered you to leave Srebrenica? Or wasn't there any order?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got two orders, the first one dated from mid-March 1993 and was issued by the commander of the 2nd Corps, General Hazim Sadic. And it was Naser Oric who personally handed the order to me. After having read it, I said that I wanted to establish a radio link with General Sadic from the post office, and this was in fact done the following day. And I, speaking to General Sadic, said that I wasn't prepared to leave Srebrenica, and that I refused to carry out the order for as long as another surgeon was sent to Srebrenica to replace me and to assume my duties. You have to know that this was the period of the most intense attack on Srebrenica, when the wounded were flowing in daily, and I was simply unable to abandon the wounded. The second order was issued on the 19th or 20th of April, 1993, and was served on me personally by a pilot of an UNPROFOR helicopter. The order stated that I should be ensured safe passage to return to Tuzla in order to be assigned to other war assignments. This took place at the time of the evacuation of the wounded from the hospital in Srebrenica, and this was done by airlift, with UNPROFOR helicopters. Over -- some 60 wounded were evacuated by helicopters and some 600 by UNPROFOR trucks. Following a complete evacuation of the wounded, I left Srebrenica on the 22nd of April, 1993, and reported to General Sadic in the late afternoon hours, in the building of the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Mujkanovic, before I hand you over to Mr. Jones, did you ever inquire why, at such a critical moment, you were being transferred? Did it seem strange to you? Did you try to find out why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reassigned from Srebrenica to Tuzla on the 22nd of April, 1993, following the demilitarisation of Srebrenica on the 17th of April, 1993. It was on that day that the Canadian Battalion arrived in Srebrenica and all the military operations were brought to a halt. The peace-making process and the demilitarising process commenced, and that was when I left Srebrenica. And I handed the hospital into the hands of a Belgian organisation, medical organisation, that entered Srebrenica in late April 1993, and they were to fully assume responsibility for those who were injured, wounded, or ill in the hospital. At the time of the first order, asking that I be ensured safe passage from Srebrenica, this order basically was a result of a constant pressure exerted by my family, by my wife. You have to know that I left my wife and my three-year-old son in Tuzla. On the 14th of July, 1992, he turned three, and that's when I left him, and then I saw him only a year later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, some questions which I may ask you may seem pretty obvious, and it may be that you feel that you've dealt with some of them already, so in that case, feel free just to confirm or deny, with a brief answer, and don't feel obliged to repeat anything, since we have a record of what you've said. But, of course, if you think there's something important to add, then please feel free to do so. I'm going to start with, actually, one question, just touching on --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed, if I may be allowed just a couple of minutes to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want a break? Do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a short break. We will reconvene when we are advised from the Victims and Witnesses Unit that we can reconvene. Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.11 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a short submission, to put it on the record. We started cross-examination, and we are prior put on notice of the exhibits to be used by Defence counsel. On the exhibits' list there is a mentioning of a video, referring to that video. We have not seen that video. We have asked several times, several days, for a copy of that video. And earlier in this trial, we already, several times, for the record, also stated that we haven't received a video. So we are not prepared, whenever this video is shown, to react on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, yes, we notified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We notified the Prosecution that we would be using a video exhibit. We have technical problems about copying videos. We simply don't have the equipment to do it. I would just note that the Prosecution won't be re-examining for several days. They'll have plenty of time to react, if there's anything they want to raise as far as the video is concerned. But it's a real problem for us to actually make copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you could have brought that to the attention of the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the agreement was that we would notify the Prosecution of what exhibits we intend to use. We have fully complied with that obligation. As to making copies, I didn't realise it would be such an issue, for a start.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my opinion, whenever it is a P or a D number, no copies are needed, but it is a practice and a ruling by your Trial Chamber that there should be provided a copy whenever it's known. And we have been sent this list for several days, and reiterated our request for several times, and still we don't have received any video. So I don't know what's in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You reiterated -- let's make this clear. You reiterated your request to the Defence, not to us, because this is the first time this is being raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So -- well, I think it needs to be addressed before we see this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The system, as you know, is no longer the one that used to be. It's not to take everyone by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no surprise tactically here at all, and you'll see when the video is played there is absolutely no element of surprise in that sense. There is a problem with us copying videos. I realise that that's something which now needs to be resolved, and hopefully that's something we can see with the technical booth and with Your Honours. I think it would be unfair for my cross-examination to be interrupted by me not being permitted to play a video which is very much built into the sequence of the questions I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think in that case, we'll start with the video, we see it. If you've had this problem of not being able to copy it and give a copy -- and give a copy to the Prosecution, what I suggest we do is we give the witness a rest, we send him back to his room or to the hotel. How long is this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- may I make the following proposal, because we've had examination-in-chief for two and a half days. I'm just embarking on my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't started, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, if I've started. I'm completely sympathetic to the witness' difficulties, and we have no problem at all with him having a break. This video is so innocuous so that for it to require us to adjourn for the witness to go back to his total, for so much time to be lost would be, in my submission, really not be an effective use of time and resources. If -- if need be, I can not use the video today, I can use it tomorrow, and perhaps at the end of this session we can see the video, the witness could leave maybe ten minutes before the end and we can see the video and decide whether I can -- whether I might be permitted today show him this video, which is an interview with him. But I do think that my learned friend is making a song and a dance about something which is really not -- is not a big -- big deal, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have transcripts. The transcript has been distributed. They can see the transcript. It's about two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, the transcript is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. We can distribute it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the speakers please make breaks between their speeches. The interpreters can't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please allow --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, I will start again, Your Honour. In fact, so -- if this is a transcript, I don't know. It will be the first time I will see such a copy. I haven't read it. Second is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long -- one moment. How long is the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The video is three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then let's see it straightaway, because we are wasting more time than discussing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could just have a look at it. If it's an interview with the witness himself, I think he can even stay here and watch it, and then you won't even have to play it again later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If there's any prejudice to the Prosecution, they can quite simply raise that once they've seen the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- what Defence counsel is pleading is that I should rely on his judgement for what is in the video, that I should rely on my strategy for the Prosecution, what is the content. And then the length of the video does not matter. It is what is in it. And it is also the possibility for the Prosecution to prepare itself for such a cross -- sorry, such a re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's put it like this: There is no question about this. If, under normal circumstances, you have a right to re-examine the witness, multo magis, when you have something like this happen, that right stands -- stands out. So you don't have to worry about any prejudice, because at the end of the day, you always have the right to re-examine the witness on this video, particularly if you feel like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when it is so -- so short in time, then it means that I might request you for that period of time to see it before the cross-examination start, so that will take five minutes, ten minutes, but only before the cross-examination will start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely what I was going to suggest, but the two of you didn't let me finish. What I'm going to suggest is this: I didn't know what this video was all about, I didn't know that it was an interview with -- of the witness, to start with. So that explains why I said we'll see it in his absence. But if it's -- if he himself is being interviewed, there is no point in even seeing it in his absence. He can stay here, and that will economise in time because he won't need to see it again later, that's number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number two is this: Given that, to an extent, the Prosecution is being taken by "surprise" in the sense as regards the contents of this video, then if they need a short break to check for themselves whatever they need to check before you proceed with your cross-examination, then I think it's the case of saying yes. If it's the case of proceeding with the cross-examination straightaway and delaying the series of questions on this video, or arising out of this video, until tomorrow, then we would be able to meet, perhaps, the concerns of the Prosecution in that manner, without the need to have another break today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's do it that way. I'll only deal with the video tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And so you will have ample time to check on this, and of course later on to re-examine the witness if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And when will we take a copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he's going to tender it, you can have a copy made today by the staff of the Tribunal. I understand they can do it -- if it's not a long video, they can do it in minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That means for Defence counsel that he's able to provide us fast with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do we really need Mr. Wubben's wrestling with anger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, let's please get on with it. Does the technical booth have a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're going to play it from where? From there, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into video evidence, I suppose, or computer evidence. Computer evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make this clear: You don't have any objection, Mr. Wubben, for the witness to remain here while this is being shown, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, I have no objection, first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you don't have an objection, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't imagine that you would. So let's proceed, please. Thank you. And thank you for your cooperation, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to play the opening titles, and then the section that we're going to show -- there's no point in showing the whole programme. Just to show the introduction and then the segment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] [As read] Well, no. Ever since Naser was taken to The Hague, I had no direct contacts with him. I had certain indirect contacts, through people who went there and saw him, and then came back. So we are in indirect contact. I had no direct conversations with him, and I was with Naser the whole time that I stayed in Srebrenica. It means that I factually fought in war under his command. I think all the best about him as a person and as a commander. Question: What is your standpoint, is Naser guilty or not? Mujkanovic: I wouldn't like to take competencies of the Tribunal or anyone else. Certainly, Srebrenica, the very concept of fighting the war and the attempt by this enclave to survive in the area of central Podrinje, which covered the area of some 200 kilometres from Zvornicka Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kamenica to Zepa. Sometimes people don't have a clue. They think it was a surrounded town. It was factually an enclave that was liberated at a certain point in time, except for the very town of Bratunac. I'm talking strictly about the town of Bratunac, not villages and hamlets around Bratunac. By Drina, or as they say, downstream of Drina, practically from Zvornik all the way to Zepa. During my visit to war health outposts and hospitals in Zepa, I even went to Zupa Visegradska, to the right bank of Drina. This was a huge territory. It was very difficult to control the area. It was very difficult to organise it in accordance with all the postulates, the Geneva Convention - as someone nowadays calls it - warfare, et cetera. People there fought for survival against the invasion by the Serb-Montenegrin enemy, as they called it at the time. At the same time, it was a battle for survival, battle against hunger, because for a long time this enclave didn't receive any food, medicines or medical supplies, and it was very, very difficult to survive there. People literally died of starvation. Question: Doctor, will everyone ever find out the truth about Srebrenica? Mujkanovic: Just as I said before -- you see, among all the inhabitants of Srebrenica, everyone has their own truth. According to estimates, there were between 80.000 and 100.000 people there at the time, women, children, old people. There was both the army and civilians, and it was very difficult to separate soldiers from civilians -- everybody was one or the other at a certain point. Everyone has his or her own truth about Srebrenica. And I think that it is good, because everyone saw the truth differently, in a way as it happened to them. So it's factually impossible to find out the truth about Srebrenica, the pure truth. It is always coloured by emotions. If you say that the destiny of Srebrenica was the one like in 1995 - an enclave turned over to the Republika Srpska army - and that the crime was committed and that it is still investigated as to who and how committed the crime, and that all the names of the 7.000 or 8.000 people who were killed there are still not known -- it means that it always has this dimension of the committed crime, and then probably in that moment, people do not want to reveal some other things. It is like a barrier, because if someone committed a crime, then nobody has the right to investigate anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's the segment we proposed to show. After that there's a discussion of Bianca Jagger and Mick Jagger, which we can probably skip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you for showing, and we won't take the opportunity for further delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Do I take that to mean that if Mr. Jones wants to fire questions on this video today, he can do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Tomorrow, as discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow, all right. Thank you. Let's proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, firstly, are you okay to continue now?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, first, just a couple of questions about the last subject you were asked about, which was the evacuation of the wounded in April 1993. Isn't it right that the Serbs actually shelled the evacuation of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that among the people being evacuated were a number of people, including children, who had been on the 12th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There was a terrible shelling that day, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little about that?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in early April 1993 when there was an overall attack on Srebrenica. Prior to that, Cerska and Konjevic Polje had fallen, so the entire population from those areas was transferred to the town of Srebrenica, which meant that some 15.000 or more people had arrived and they were accommodated in the primary and secondary schools in Srebrenica. Some of them were accommodated on the streets before some more adequate accommodation could be found for them. On that day, in front of the school, it was a sunny day, people were sitting outside. There were a lot of refugees there. Six or seven shells were fired from a multiple rocket-launcher to that place, to the school. This resulted in a huge massacre, and over 100 people were killed on that occasion, and approximately the same number were seriously injured. It was about half past two in the afternoon. There were UNPROFOR members there as well. They helped us to move the injured people in their APCs and transport them to the hospital, which was about 400 or 500 metres away. Among the injured people there were lots of women and lots of children. There were also men. The situation was terrible. I know that at 3.00, I started my first operation, and I ended my last one 36 hours later. All this time I was in the operating theatre. I remember a young boy who had lost his eyes through shrapnel fire. I believe that his name was either Bekric or Bektic Sead. This young boy, later on, was transported to Tuzla, and from there he was adopted. And I believe that he currently resides in the United States of America. The situation was horrible, and it's very difficult for me to go back in time at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be fair to say that you probably left Srebrenica because you were completely burnt out after your -- after eight months, or however long it was that you were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so. The road to Srebrenica was so difficult, so dangerous, but the stay in Srebrenica was no less dangerous or difficult. Getting to Srebrenica was only half the job; the other half was actually being in Srebrenica. I've already said in my testimony that there was -- there were attempts to get additional medical teams to Srebrenica, but this always failed. Seven doctors were killed, and a lot of nurses. Every attempt to get additional people into Srebrenica by road failed. There were a lot of people who fell victim to those attempts. On the 3rd of May, a team in the helicopter died somewhere between Zepa and Sekovici. The helicopter was gunned down, and everybody on the helicopter killed as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for clarification, the Belgian organisation which took over or which sent doctors was Medicine sans Frontieres, right, or MSF?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was the Belgian branch of the Medicine sans Frontieres. The head of that organisation was Eric Dachy. I met that man. In the month of March, together with General Morillon, he arrived helped me in my work. He even assisted me with some surgeries. And then after the 22nd of April, I handed the war hospital over into their hands. On my return, I was returned to the war hospital from which I had left for Srebrenica. This was Kalesija. I was closer to home, I could visit my family every day, I could spend time with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, but Eric Dachy, you had already met in 1992, and you had already worked with him about getting medicines to the hospital; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I met Eric Dachy was in late November 1992. He entered with the first convoy. His task was to take stock of the situation in the hospital and see how the Medicine sans Frontieres could be of help with the overall functioning of the hospital and the medical corps in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I apologise if I seem to be cutting you off sometimes, but I'm conscious that you probably want to return to Tuzla before too long, so I'll try and keep the answers short. Now, I've got some general questions, and then I'm going back to the beginning of what you told us. Now, you may now that Naser Oric is charged with, among other things, failing to prevent looting, stealing chickens, cows, and other goods. So my question to you is this: Do you think Naser Oric could have prevented civilians from stealing those things during military actions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, no speculation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, he's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As you said "do you think," so he needs to give a carefully -- a careful answer, in other words, thinking based on reasoning, not on speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. He's already given a lot of evidence about the problems of these civilians, so really that's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In your opinion, based on your experience, do you think that Naser Oric, or anyone, could have prevented that happening? I'd be grateful if the witness could answer before he's interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But now it's added another kind of speculation, "or anyone else." This is too wide for speculation, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on Naser Oric. Yes, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want me to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony so far, over the past two days, I have said that the entire area of Srebrenica - and you could hear it in the interview that you showed at the beginning - I said that the entire area of Srebrenica was an unorganised area. Nobody could look after these people in the way it could be expected. There were no conditions in place for any kind of normal life. There was no food; nobody could provide it. I have to tell you, irrespective of any actions that were undertaken by the troops in order to reach certain villages, to get hold of food or some other things, people would sneak up to the Serbian villages during the night and loot the wheat and grain storages.
