The civilians would do that during the night. One night it would be one group of people; the second night, this group would be joined by a few more people. And the Serbs knew that, and on the third night they would plant mines in the area. And I had a lot more problems in the hospital treating civilians who were injured by booby traps, because it would happen that they would enter a minefield and they would be brought into the hospital wounded, multi-traumatised. In my view, in that short period of chaos, which involved a large number of refugees and large number of people who had been transferred two or three times from their original place of residence, in that short period of time, nobody could organise any way of normalcy that is linked with a normal geopolitical situation. Not only Naser Oric, nobody - nobody - could look after these people. These people were left to their own means. Everybody was left to look after themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So may I take it that the answer is no, he couldn't prevent that happening? Just to summarise.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there wasn't, and there could not have been, any authority or organisation, be it the War Presidency or an individual, who could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would the same apply for the destruction of Serb property?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already explained that the things that happened with regard to the Serbian property, houses, furniture, food. This was mostly caused by the civilians who wanted to get hold of food and things that they thought could be used in barter, that would eventually, again, end up with them getting food. And that was the biggest problem of the Srebrenica enclave. There was no mechanism, there was no instrument that could have prevented that from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I didn't interrupt, but again, this is a kind of speculation, and this is not testifying about facts that the witness saw but an opinion, a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue. I've made it clear that the questions that are being made and answered by the witness are not to solicit opinions based on speculation but opinions based on facts, so I don't think we are in the realm of speculation as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Finally, as far as you're aware, with your contacts with Naser Oric, he never encouraged these practices, never encouraged burning or looting.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already confirmed that in my testimony. I said that not only did he not encourage, he saw it as a problem that was a constant subject of discussion at the War Presidency. Naser Oric's position was that there shouldn't be any fire set to the property. But nobody could prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going back to the beginning. I'll try and take these points as quickly as possible. You were cut short when you began to tell of your trip into Srebrenica in late July, early August 1992. You basically told us that you got in on the fourth attempt. Now, I won't ask you to go into the details of that journey now. Would you agree that it was incredibly hard for you to get into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible, to all intents and purposes. I don't know, if I were in the same situation today, I would probably never do it again. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm going to break it up. And is that because the Serbs had extremely strong lines around Srebrenica which you had to crawl through, crawling through land-mines and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire area of the central Podrinje enclave was intersected. It was not one continuum. The first part that was held by the Serbs was around the Zvornik municipality. There was a zone composed of Snagovo and Kamenica, composed of Muslim villages that managed to defend themselves from the aggression at first. And then there was another interruption after which was the area of Cerska and Konjevic Polje. This was one sort of a continuum, but in certain places, this continuum was very questionable. Between Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica, there was Kravica which interrupted that continuum. On several occasions, I would manage to get into the territory controlled by the Serbs, and I would manage to leave that territory and get to the free territory. It was a very difficult journey. My life was at risk. And you could see it yourself, that in December, a whole column that wanted to take the same road was killed together with the two doctors and the medical team that was part of that column.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't you and Nurif and his men, on some occasions, literally have to crawl on your hands and knees, single-file, to get through Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And weren't you ambushed on the way in, and people from your group were wounded?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning we were ambushed, and one of the people who were in charge of the war hospital was wounded. There were some 50 people who were employed by the war hospital. There was shelling. There were injuries on that road. We had to go through minefields. This journey took six days and six nights, and the distance is only about 80 kilometres, as the crow flies. And you had to travel for six or seven days, sometimes even longer. So you can see it yourself, that this was a very dangerous journey to take, involving huge risks for anybody's life.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you hear, as you were coming in, on Radio Zvornik that the Serbs were aware of your presence but they were exaggerating your numbers and saying that you were 4.000 Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. As I said, if you can keep your answers short - I'm sorry if I cut you off - but we do need to make progress.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And from your time -- let me put it this way: Was that the sort of typical Serb propaganda which you were hearing at the time, exaggerating the organisation and the strength of the Muslim forces? Is that something you were familiar with, that phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And equally, didn't Serb propaganda typically understate the organisation and strength of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I don't want to you speculate here. You're either sure about this or you're not, Dr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they are understated their organisation. However, I know that they exaggerated our numbers. Listening to the news in the morning, when we were getting ready to get into the area of Srebrenica, we were listening to the Radio Zvornik news, and it was said that in Nezuk, where we were, there were 4.000 Green Berets. That's how they called Bosniaks and Muslims at the time. And they said that their mission was to infiltrate themselves into the territory of Zenica. It was a long time ago. It's very difficult for me to remember the exact wording of the news. But I know that the figure that was mentioned at the time was 4.000 Green Berets, and the number was five or six times more than it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this situation that you've described of Srebrenica being physically cut off, if I can put it that way, from Tuzla, wasn't that true for the whole period of the war, from the start of the war to the final genocide in Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely so. I believe that on the 17th of April, 1992, Srebrenica was taken by the Serbs, and from that moment on, even to this very day, it has been practically cut off. And that situation was the same in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you were asked yesterday about reports - that was the word being used - sent to Sarajevo and Tuzla, and you spoke of appeals on the radio for medicines and equipment, telling the world about the shelling that was happening and whatnot. Now, firstly, was this by what was called ham radio, amateur radio?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a ham radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it was an open line which anyone could listen in on.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an amateur radio station which was in the building of the post office in Srebrenica. It was manned by Ibrahim Becirevic. And I used it on two or three occasions when I spoke with my family in Tuzla. I also spoke with General Sadic using that radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wasn't it also manned by Naser, not Naser Oric but another Naser, who was manning the radio?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another man and his name was Naser. I don't know his last name. There was this guy Becirevic, whose first name was Ibrahim. There was this guy called Naser, whose last name I don't know. And there was also Hamid, whose last name was Alic, I believe, and he also worked in the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the radio, firstly, it's an obvious point, but the Serbs could hear what was being said on the ham radio; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, my question is: These -- would you agree that these were more like appeals for help to the outside world rather than a report from a subordinate to a superior? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I explained that -- how these reports were sent from this radio station. They were either aired directly or were first recorded on the Radio Sarajevo or Television Sarajevo or some local stations, such as Radio Tuzla, so on and so forth. And then at the time that news was aired, and that was every hour on the hour at 7.00 and then 10.00, these reports were heard and they usually were read about Ibrahim Becirevic. Those reports spoke about the humanitarian situation, the need for medicines, the number of injured and killed, the shelling of Srebrenica, and assistance was requested. And this happened almost every day, or at least two or three days every week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right to consider these reports in the sense of, I don't know, a news report on a disaster, like the tsunami which we've heard about recently, saying what's happening and appealing for help to be brought in? Would you accept that characterisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but a report for help can also contend other information. This is too general, and then it becomes too speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A report can be anything. That's why I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you be more specific in your question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You're familiar, Dr. Mujkanovic, with news reports which we see on television? It's just a simple question.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference between those news reports and our news reports. Ours were drafted by amateurs. They were sometimes aired directly. And they spoke about the situation as it was. I could hardly compare the quality of our reports with the quality of other reports written by journalists. In any case, our reports spoke about the humanitarian situations, about requirements, about shelling, the number of killed and wounded, about the attacks. Those reports were all aimed at requesting help for Srebrenica, help in food, medicines, and so on and so forth. Maybe one could come by some of these reports so that you could hear what they looked like. They were aired directly via local radio, such as Radio Tuzla or even Radio Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's pretty clear, and I don't want to labour the point, but I'll draw a distinction because the word "report" does have two senses. Firstly, a report where a situation is being described, where information is being provided to the wider world, let's say, and then a report in the sense of someone reporting to another person because they have a duty to describe what's happening. Now, the reports which you've described, these appeals for help, are they more the first type of report, i.e., providing information and appealing for assistance, or a report in the second sense, i.e., someone having to report to a superior what the situation is? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's pretty much confusing. Let's leave it where it is, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's see if he understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's already explained what this is. This is a news item which also contains appeals for help addressed to whoever wants to lend an ear to such appeals. But we are not talking of reports in the sense of -- the second sense that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's already covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't wish to belabour the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us on Monday that Nurif Rizvanovic, who travelled with you from Tuzla, stayed in Konjevic Polje. Now, he was originally from Glogova, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he and his unit stay in Konjevic Polje because they planned to help the Muslim fighters in Bratunac fight against the Serbs, including --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now the Muslim enclave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because the witness' answer was not heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last answer.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, wasn't the Muslim enclave of Konjevic Polje cut off from Srebrenica at the time, at the time you arrived, so that you would have to cross Serb lines to get from Konjevic Polje to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was cut off. There was no physical continuum between Konjevic Polje and the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if people wanted to get from one enclave to the other, didn't they have to undertake a dangerous trek through woods and hills, running the risk of Serb ambushes?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that's what couriers would have to do if they were going to get a message to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And equally, wasn't the Muslim enclave of Cerska completely cut off from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was cut off from -- in the relation to Srebrenica, but it was territorially connected with Konjevic Polje. It was, however, cut off from Srebrenica, because first you had Cerska, then Konjevic Polje, and then Srebrenica, if you take it from the north to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, if we start from the very north, you would have Kamenica as well, wouldn't you, which was cut off from Srebrenica but maybe had continuity with Cerska.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kamenica neither. Kamenica wasn't really connected territorial with Cerska, because when you look at Srebrenica, then you have Snagovo and then Kamenica. Between Kamenica and Cerska, there was this one swathe that was very narrow where you had to pass almost through the Serb territory. It was a very dangerous passage. And, of course, Kamenica was physically cut off from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And wasn't that the situation until Kravica was taken on the 7th of January, 1993, when finally there was continuity between Kravica and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After Kravica was taken over, there was the physical continuum between Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica, so that the route between the two could be taken safely, of course not along the road, because that meant going through Bratunac in the direction of Konjevic Polje. But there were safe passages across hills and through forest, all the way to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, as I said, I'm going to ask some general questions about the situation, and please feel free just to say yes or no or to give a short answer, if you can. When you arrived in Srebrenica, would you agree that it was under siege by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would you agree that the reason why Srebrenica existed as an enclave is because the Serbs had ethnically cleansed all the Muslims from the surrounding areas and they had flooded into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely what I've been saying in the past few days. Srebrenica was the place of refuge for the refugees from Han Pijesak, which is far off from Srebrenica, to the local areas, like Bratunac, Vlasenica, Zvornik, and of course parts of the Srebrenica municipality, meaning the villages around Srebrenica that were part of the Srebrenica municipality, where the population fled from their homes and went to the town proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And so is it right that there were refugees arriving all the time, every day, and that it was impossible, effectively, to keep track of who was actually in the enclave at any given time?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't as many flowing in. But from the direction of Zepa, the refugees would trickle in almost every day, and Zepa is a small village to the south of Srebrenica. These refugees would first come to Zepa from the areas of Visegrad, Han Pijesak, Gorazde. They would take this first leg of the journey to Zepa, but Zepa was very small. And they expected Srebrenica, being a town, that there they would have greater possibilities of finding accommodation. And that's why they would arrive on a daily basis. Sometimes there would be 10 of them a day, sometimes 20 a day, sometimes none. But anyway, they would be coming to Srebrenica. But this flow ran uninterrupted, particularly from mid-February until April 1993, when Cerska and Konjevic Polje fell and the south-eastern part of Srebrenica, all those villages along the Drina, and that's when the town became an impossible place to live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you speak to many of these refugees and hear stories from them about what had happened to them and why they had come to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not talk to these refugees much. You see, I had the opportunity of speaking to them when they were patients of mine, or to talk to the families of my patients when they came visiting. And that's when I heard stories of them having been driven out, villages torched, members of their families killed. These stories were horrendous. But I did not really talk to the refugees in terms of interviewing them. There were many wounded from Zepa who I operated on and treated, who came downstream along the Drina River from the Zepa area. They came downstream and were from there taken by trucks to the hospital. These were both civilians and soldiers who got wounded up there and required serious treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did -- well, let me put it this way: We've heard Serb witnesses saying that Muslims left their homes because they didn't want to live with the Serbs anymore, that they just left voluntarily. Is that reflected in the conversations which you had in Srebrenica with refugees?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, on the subject of weaponry, would you agree that the Serb forces surrounding and besieging Srebrenica possessed superior weaponry to the Muslims in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would definitely agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that they were -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question has quite a simple answer, because the Serb army, that is, the JNA, was the force waging the war in Srebrenica. The entire military hardware possessed by the JNA was in the hands of the Serb army. Now, whether you call it the Serb army, the army of the VRS, or the JNA, they had the -- they had aircraft, they had long-barrelled weapons. And this is something that UNPROFOR soldiers can confirm to you, because they saw it with their own eyes. Around a thousand shells hit Srebrenica daily. There were more than 50 or 60 air raids against such a small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As I say, I apologise if the questions seem obvious -- if the answers seem obvious, but I do need to go through it. In terms of heavy artillery, would you agree that the Serbs had heavy artillery positioned on the high points, the surrounding hills, north, east, south, and west, around the enclave?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as the period of time which is relevant -- with a view to strategy of Defence takes a long time, and it's unclear for me what time period he's testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're 100 per cent right. I'm sure Mr. Jones will agree with that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Wasn't that true during the whole time you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak for the period when I was there, from 5 August until the 17th of April. That's the period I can vouch for and confirm for. And it is in relation to that period that I'm saying that Srebrenica came under attack daily, from long-distance, multiple rocket-launchers. I know that multiple rocket-launchers were used to hit the Srebrenica Hospital. It was -- I don't know which elevation point, trigometric point it was. But you can hear them being fired, one, two, three, four, and then the salvo hitting the hospital. This was on a hill that was completely razed. And I saw with my own eyes, the aviation bombing Srebrenica. It was for an entire month that, at five past three in the afternoon, the planes would have their sorties to attack Srebrenica. And I can speak for the period from 5 August until the 17th of April, the time I spent in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And speaking -- and I don't specify a period, you can assume that I'm asking about the whole period you were there. Isn't it right that the Muslims, the Bosniaks, had practically no artillery except for what they could capture from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. When I came to Srebrenica, I found it a bit strange that one rifle was to be shared by three soldiers. The weaponry they possessed were mostly infantry weapons. There was no artillery at the time, nor any heavy machine-guns. There were even homemade, makeshift rifles, and that's a fact. This period was characterised by such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Such weapons made from pipes of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Leave it at makeshift. I mean it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'm just trying to get a sense of how improvised they were. Fine. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Didn't also, due to the shortage of weapons and ammunition, didn't people often take weapons off the dead, off dead Serbs or dead Muslims, just in order that they would have a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I don't want you to speculate again. You either have this information directly by having seen it, or indirectly by being told so. Otherwise, please don't speculate.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question, Mr. President. I don't know how people came by their weapons, whether they took them off the dead or not. I can't really say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right that the weapons were very valuable commodities at the time?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, a few questions about uniforms, and apologies, again, because you have dealt with it at length. But today the Prosecution seemed to suggest that uniforms were worn during actions. I'm not sure if that was a summary, if that was your evidence. It's right, isn't it, that in the actions, most people did not have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained the matter in relation to the uniforms worn in Srebrenica, that perhaps some 10 per cent of all had some sort of a camouflage uniform, whereas 90 per cent of them had civilian clothes mixed with, perhaps, some military dress. They would have a jacket, they would have gym shoes, and so on. And when we talk about uniforms in Srebrenica, I have to tell you that the army wasn't uniformed. Whatever they had on them, they would appear in those clothes at their positions, go back home, go to town in. Those were their everyday clothes. These weren't any uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Taking the other side of the coin, if you saw someone who actually did have a uniform, would that necessarily mean that he was in the military, or could it be simply that he possessed combat fatigues?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it wouldn't mean really that they were a member of the army or in the military. I can, for instance, tell you about the people who came with me to Srebrenica from Tuzla. They were my escorts, and they wore this -- these -- this camouflage uniform. But they weren't actually soldiers, they weren't a member of any unit going to a front line. So this wasn't an absolute rule, although most of those who wore some sort of a uniform were soldiers. But there were those who wore uniforms without actually being members of any units. I have to explain this to you in more detail. I think it's important for this Trial Chamber to understand this. It was left up to the people in Srebrenica to decide whether they want to be soldiers or not, because there was no way you could force them to become one. If you wanted to force them to become a soldier, you have to provide them with a gun, with a rifle, and you don't have one. Then the person is going to say, Okay, but then you have to provide me with meals, you have to take care of my family, and then I will go and man the positions. So in essence, this was on a voluntary basis, take it or leave. For instance, I, and all of my medical colleagues, could simply say, We don't want to work in the hospital anymore. Why not? Because we don't have any medicines, we don't have any medical supplies. And nobody would have been able to force us to perform our duties. It was left to a person's conscience, conscientiousness, whether they were driven by their sense of duty and integrity. But in general, you couldn't force people to do that. There were some of those who weren't members of the army at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That is a very helpful clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. The other matter, and just bearing in mind the conversation this morning, is that I'm moving on to an exhibit which we've notified the Prosecution about. It's an extract of a book which was in the public domain. I have just checked with my case manager, and we have copies here, so perhaps if the Prosecution has that during the break -- they no doubt -- well. I won't speculate on whether they've seen the book before but it's -- it's War Hospital by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not my business to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't receive photocopies, so we made them ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So I'll be moving on to that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for taking a longer break, but we didn't have a break at all, we were discussing something that we will need to discuss with both of you next week in camera. You will receive a communication my legal officer in due course, all right? But there will be a meeting next week, towards the end, either Thursday or Friday of next week, and that will be after the sitting. You will be informed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed. Again, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I'm going to be asking you now and tomorrow about a book called War Hospital, this book by Sheri Fink, with which I'm sure you're familiar.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just by way of housekeeping, practically, there are a number of pages from this book which I intend to refer to. Rather than exhibiting each page, I've put them together in a bundle. But realising that even a bundle might be incoherent for Your Honours, I actually have copies of the book, the whole book, four copies, which I can provide for each of Your Honours and one for the Registry. I can do that tomorrow. I don't have them with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It seems one way of proceeding rather than copying the whole thing. So I'll have copies tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And one question in that regard, Dr. Mujkanovic, do you read English?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a certain command of English, but I don't speak as fluently as you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see. I'll read out sections, and I'll also provide a copy so that you can have that in front of you. Now, is it right, firstly, that Dr. Sheri Fink interviewed you at length when she was writing the book?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sheri Fink is a lady doctor from the United States of America, and in early 1998, she came to Tuzla. Reportedly, she had a project of writing a book about the war hospital in Srebrenica. We conversed for some two or three years, of course intermittently, because she would be there and then we would speak for some ten days and then she would go back to the States. So yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And isn't it that this story that you've been telling us today, and yesterday, and the day before about the situation in Srebrenica is pretty much what you told Dr. Sheri Fink when she interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the story I was saying in 1993, 1995, in 1998, so that's how I saw the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, the first section which I'm going to look at, it's just on the subject of uniforms which you were discussing before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should distribute copies, first of all, with the usher's assistance. Yes, and I have a copy also for the stenographer. I can provide my copy to the shorthand writer. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could a copy be given to the court assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm endeavouring to arrange now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it's -- the first section I want to turn to is pages 63 to 64, and I'll just -- I'll just start reading it. It says: "That day he," and he's referring to Dr. Ilijas Pilav, whom you've mentioned, "carried his weapons and wore what had become his typical battle uniform - a white bandanna around his forehead and his old, black gym suit. Fatima," and that refers to Fatima Delbasic [phoen], "knew that gym suit well ..."

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't know if you heard the section I read out. If so, I don't need to read it again. It says: "That day he," Pilav," carried his weapons and wore what had become his typical uniform - a white bandanna around his forehead and his old, black gym suit. Fatima," and that's Fatima Delbasic, "knew that gym suit well ..." My question is this: Do you agree that Srebrenica's fighters, and that includes in that instance Dr. Pilav, would wear suits like that for battle, a black gym suit, a blue policeman's uniforms, a former factory worker's overalls, old JNA uniforms, basically whatever was at hand?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I've been saying. There were no standardised uniforms in Srebrenica. A uniform meant whatever clothes one had and would then wear. So I agree that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've explained how the armed forces or the defence forces were improvised. Wasn't it more common at the time to refer to fighters, borci, rather than soldiers, vojnici, when describing Srebrenica's defenders?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used the term "borci," fighters, we never used the term "vojnici," soldiers. I even told you that they identified themselves with their commanders. If they were Hakim's fighters, then they would be Hakimnovci, or Zulfo's fighters. The term "vojnici," soldiers, was never used, only the term "borci," fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In terms of proper uniforms, i.e., uniforms with distinctive insignia or with some uniformity, didn't they come from Nurif -- for the first time, come with Nurif Rizvanovic and his men, that they had some proper uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I met Nurif Rizvanovic in the second half of July 1992, in the locality of Nezuka, where he was assigned as escort to ensure the passage of myself and those who were carrying the equipment for the war hospital to Srebrenica. That was the first time that I ever saw uniformed military, those that had uniforms, boots, badges on their hats. It was a unit that was 470 strong. They wore camouflage uniforms, cachets with the badge of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with lilies, with military boots and all the attendant weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's Nurif's men, is that correct, and they stayed in Konjevic Polje, after you went into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just while I'm on the subject of your arriving in Srebrenica, isn't it right that you brought the seal, a stamp, with you when you came into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal stamp as a medical doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that the stamp which you brought in, or was there a military stamp which you brought with you into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had my own stamp of a medical doctor that I normally used in my practice. I had no other stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Actually, it may -- might have been, and only answer if you're aware, did Nurif bring a stamp, a military-type stamp, from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of questions on -- on these bands, these strings of cloth which you mentioned which were sometimes used in actions. Is it right, firstly, that those were used so that the people in the actions wouldn't get shot at by their own people?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a sign of recognition for the fighters who went into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've agreed that the fighters lived at home very often with their families and other refugees, and that that's how those civilians would learn of actions. To your knowledge, did civilians themselves sometimes wear these pieces of cloth when they went into actions for the very same reason, to avoid getting shot at?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, about the civilians wearing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But would you know for sure, if you saw someone with a piece of cloth, that he was part of an organised unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that for sure. It wasn't the sort of thing where you could be sure that someone who wasn't part of the unit was not going to wear it. But it was a way for those who took part together in action to recognise each other, probably the only possible way to distinguish your own men from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, I'm going to come to Hakija's unit for a moment, but leaving his unit aside, isn't it right that there were no barracks, no armoury, none of the typical features which you expect of a regular army in Srebrenica when you were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the units had any barracks, armouries, or anything of the sort. The fighters stayed in their homes, and it was from there that they manned the positions and then went back. It was only Hakija's men who were put up at the Hotel Domavija. I myself stayed at that hotel and worked in the hospital. So I met these people in the hotel every day, and I know that there they had their own premises. Since this unit was made up of fighters from the town of Srebrenica, I know for a fact that they often went to their homes and then returned to the hotel, so not even they stayed in the hotel only as a regular army. It wasn't any sort of a barracks for them. They would simply come and go as they pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And since you mentioned Hakija and his unit, would you agree that he was an independent commander, that is, independent of Naser Oric, for one, not under Naser Oric's control?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And Hakija didn't report to Naser, did he?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And neither did Hakija's men, then. They were neither under Oric's command and control.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How many of Hakija's men were there, roughly, in the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent I knew from staying at the hotel, there were perhaps some 200 to 300 men, at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And also, on the subject of Zulfo Tursunovic, you mentioned, I think on Monday, how people in Podravanje had said that Zulfo had ordered them to burn haystacks. Knowing Zulfo, do you know that to be the case, that he ordered that? Is that consistent with his character as you knew it?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw only one haystack that was set aflame. And two younger men were running across a hill slope. They came to this haystack and torched it. And when asked by Hakija not to do it, they said, "We want to do it because Zulfo told us it was okay." And I don't think Zulfo would have said it. I knew him, and I don't think that it was the way he treated property, especially this type of property. I know there was a conversation to that effect. There was a problem in Srebrenica on how to feed the cattle that the refugees brought with themselves to Srebrenica. So I wouldn't be so sure that Zulfo really told them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you came to know Zulfo while you were in Srebrenica, would you agree that he was a pretty independent character?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that he would basically do his own thing?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree, knowing Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you also agree that he didn't necessarily inform Naser Oric of what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zulfo Tursunovic's nature is as follows: He had been sentenced for a double homicide in 1975, in the former Yugoslavia, and he spent some time in prison. He was in prison up to 1989 and then he was set free. He was supposed to serve 20 years, but he was parolled. He was a strange man. He would come to Srebrenica only occasionally from the area of Suceska. It would be once a week or maybe twice sometimes, but it would be rather once a week. And nobody really wanted to have anything to do with him, or to get on his bad side. He was very determined, and when he said something, he didn't like anybody to object to what he said or defy him. And people usually thought that if Zulfo said something, then it's better just to take it as it was said and not comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He was considerably older than Naser Oric at the time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, when I met him, he was 60, 61, if I'm right -- yes, he was considerably older, at least by 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he accept Naser Oric as having any authority over him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's, Your Honour, speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It may be something he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're in a position to tell us, answer that question with a yes or no, without speculating, then do so. If you think that you could only speculate, then don't. That's the way we will go about it.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this question. I can't say whether he did or whether he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, coming back to the organisation of the forces, again, it's maybe an obvious point, but there were no salaries paid to fighters, were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What salaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And speaking of other commanders, we've spoken about --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no salaries, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's how I understood your answer. Weren't there -- leaving aside Hakija for the moment, in the whole enclave of Srebrenica, weren't there a lot of local commanders who had autonomy?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that. The units were linked with certain geographical areas. Heads of those units were people who had certain authorities -- authority over these fighters. These men trusted their leaders, and that's how they became commanders. They were not appointed, they were self-appointed commanders who were approved by the fighters who lived in certain localities, in certain villages or in certain parts of the area. And that's the relationship that they had amongst each other. If the men didn't want to do something, then they didn't do it. So there was a lot of negotiations among the so-called authorities and their men. If the men said that they didn't want to do it, they would just take their men, go back to the village. I'm talking about the leaders. And this is how the thing functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would it be right that a commander, the success of a commander, would be judged by his ability to keep the Serbs back, to defend the front lines, and to prevent the lines from falling and massacre ensuing? That was how he was judged by his people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection in the fact that the question is focusing only by one judgement and doesn't leave any space open for other judgements within an organisation or by a supreme commander or by the people who are defended or by his soldiers. So the question is unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So maybe you can rephrase the question to take into account what has been mentioned by Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was the question unclear to you, Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like you to rephrase it, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Isn't what --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt, but your question to Mr. John Jones was please rephrase your question, and Mr. Jones didn't rephrase the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, he hasn't rephrased it, because he will now certainly rephrase it because even the witness himself has told him he did not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it saves time if the witness has understood it, and that's why I asked. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The success -- would you agree that the success of a commander, a local commander, depended on his ability to repel attacks by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case, and that's how they were judged at the beginning of the war. Whoever was the bravest in the village would become commander, and he would rally fighters around him. They did not all start fighting all at once. At the beginning of the war, only small groups would put up resistance. And then when the rest of the people saw that they had successes, they would join in. And the more weapons they gathered, the more people could be armed. So people were appointed commanders or selected as commanders if they had previously done something really brave to prevent the Serb attacks on their respective villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right, then, that there wasn't a demand to have commanders who necessarily had military experience or military training, that it was really -- that that wasn't something which the people were looking for in their commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I have to interrupt. First, there is no specific date mentioning, while the witness mentioned a specific date -- specific days -- specific period of time, beginning of the war, and earlier my learned friend indicated to the witness, Whenever I don't specify in my question the dates, I mean at the time of your arrival. So this makes it very unclear, and again I protest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you need to be clear about this, Mr. Jones. Which period of time are you referring to so that I can then direct the witness to answer the question in relation to that time period or time frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, if I may, Your Honour, the witness has been describing a general impression from -- Your Honour, Mr. Wubben is on his feet before I even finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead, Mr. Jones, you are addressing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If my learned friend would give me the courtesy of sitting down while I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Mr. Jones. We are all very anxious to hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. As am I. This witness was giving his opinion which was clearly based on a number of impressions based on conversations, on what he saw, on what he observed, about how units came together in the beginning. It's something which clearly he's had the experience and the competence to speak about. If I were to try to say to him, In May 1992, were local people looking for commanders with military background or were they more concerned to have someone who was successful at fighting the Serbs? It's highly artificial. We're talking about a general process by which the armed forces of Srebrenica came together, and this witness is giving clear evidence on that, and I'm sure he has a clear answer on whether it was important to have cadre staff, military-educated officers, or successful fighters. It's a very clear issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically you're not tying it up to a particular period of time or a particular month, but you are tying it up to the early stages when these commanders were coming to light and when their units were being created.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, in particular, when I stood up whenever Defence counsel stated, well, the witness is able to put on a general remark, and that general remark, that triggers me. First, again, not to the date. The witness said the beginning of the war, and we all know at the beginning of the war, he was not in Srebrenica because he was -- started from August until January, and there again, that triggers me to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm putting an end to this. Be as specific as you can. If you can talk about this matter, about how these commanders came to be, how they became commanders from a time when you had not even arrived in Srebrenica, then do so. If you can only speak about this phenomenon, call it like that, from your -- from the time you started gaining experience on the ground in Srebrenica, then stick to that period. But I was not there, I wasn't with you. You are the one who can give us the information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived in Srebrenica, the commanders already existed, they were in place, they were active in the areas of which I have already spoken about. However, from the month of May I was in the Kalesija war hospital, and I know that the custom was in the villages around Kalesija, when resistance was first being put up, that the most courageous, the bravest men, were selected as commanders, despite the fact that most of them did not have any military education. Up to the very end of the war, none of them completed any military education whatsoever. However, they acted as commanders, because at that time, the priority was to choose as commanders those people whom other people trusted. It was only later on, in 1994 and 1995, 1996, when the main requirement was for the commanders to have military education, if that was at all possible, because there was a lack of educated staff. At the very beginning of the war, however, people organised themselves, they defended themselves. I can't say how things were done in Srebrenica because I was not there at the beginning. I, however, said that I found those people there, that they were local commanders, that they enjoyed certain authorities among the fighters and among the rest of the population, and people generally trusted them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would you say that Naser Oric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we've got two minutes left, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, this is the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you agree that Naser Oric fit squarely into that category, that he was a brave fighter and that's why he was chosen as a commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, this is speculation. No time frame. It suggests, again, that when he didn't put forward as Defence counsel in his question the time frame that it should be the stay in Srebrenica, so this make it very unclear when the witness speak about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know why you are opposing. But yes, was Mr. Oric already a commander when you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived in Srebrenica, Naser Oric was the commander of the defence of Srebrenica. That's how he introduced himself to me; that's how people referred to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know how he was appointed to that position, or who appointed him?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or how he came to be in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how he was appointed to that position. However, the events in Potocari at the beginning of the aggression on Srebrenica -- yesterday you looked at a paper saying that 14 of Arkan's men had been killed, amongst whom Arkan, who was one of the most notorious at the time, and I believe that all this gave the credibility to Naser Oric to be selected. I can't speak about the way, how it happened, or when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Had you heard of him before arriving in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard of Naser Oric as we were travelling to Srebrenica, close to Konjevic Polje. I was told then that Naser Oric was the commander of the defence of Srebrenica, and as I've already told you, I expected to see him a much older man. And when I saw him, I realised he was a boy, practically. He was only 25 at the time. And this took me by surprise, I must admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we stop here at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the witness should be made aware that we'll probably be here until the end of next week, at this rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about it. He is an important witness, like many others, and we will take as much time as we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not for me, it's the interruptions, the constant interruptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, we'll continue tomorrow. Yes, are you giving this a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it might as well be at this stage, although there will be the book tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, this document is being ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D198, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
